subject: anatomy
title: Vertebral Column Architecture and Regional Vertebrae

steps.tx: A typical vertebra comprises an anterior weight-bearing vertebral body and a posterior neural vertebral arch enclosing the vertebral foramen. The **vertebral body** features thin compact cortical bone surrounding vascular cancellous trabeculae. Its superior and inferior surfaces are capped with hyaline cartilage plates that anchor the resilient intervertebral discs.
steps.say: A typical vertebra consists of an anterior body and a posterior vertebral arch surrounding the vertebral foramen. The vertebral body contains vascular cancellous bone enclosed by a thin cortical shell. Its surfaces are capped with hyaline cartilage plates that bond to intervertebral discs.

steps.tx: Projecting posteriorly from the body, two cylindrical pedicles and two flattened laminae unite to complete the **vertebral arch**. The arch supports seven processes: one posterior spinous process, two lateral transverse processes, and four articular processes with facet joints. Concavities on the pedicles form the intervertebral foramina that transmit spinal nerves.
steps.say: Extending backwards from the body, two pedicles and two laminae meet to complete the vertebral arch. The arch anchors seven processes comprising one spinous, two transverse, and four articular processes. Grooves on the pedicles create intervertebral foramina for exiting nerves.

steps.tx: The first cervical vertebra, designated the **atlas**, lacks both a vertebral body and a spinous process, consisting simply of anterior and posterior arches joined by two lateral masses. Its kidney-shaped superior articular facets articulate with the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joints, providing the nodding motion of the head.
steps.say: The first cervical vertebra, the atlas, lacks a vertebral body and spinous process, consisting of anterior and posterior arches linked by lateral masses. Its superior facets cup the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joints to allow nodding movements.

steps.tx: The second cervical vertebra, the **axis**, is built around the dens, a stout tooth of bone projecting upward from its body. This peg represents the detached centrum of the atlas, held against its anterior arch by the transverse ligament. Broad superior facets carry the lateral masses above, while a heavy bifid spinous process anchors the muscles that steady head rotation.
steps.say: The second cervical vertebra is the axis, characterised by its vertical peg called the dens or odontoid process. The transverse ligament locks the dens against the atlas so the head can turn.

vis.caption: The dens rises from the body of the axis as the pivot post around which the atlas, carrying the head, rotates sideways. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The second cervical vertebra is the **axis**, distinguished by a robust vertical projection termed the dens, or odontoid process. Representing the phylogenetically detached body of the atlas, the dens acts as a pivot around which the atlas rotates. The transverse ligament of the atlas straps the dens against the anterior arch of C1.
steps.say: The second cervical vertebra is the axis, characterized by its vertical peg called the dens or odontoid process. Representing the absorbed body of the atlas, the dens serves as a pivot pin. The transverse ligament locks the dens against the anterior atlas arch.

steps.tx: All cervical vertebrae are identified by the presence of a **foramen transversarium** in each transverse process. In vertebrae C1 through C6, this foramen transmits the vertebral artery, vertebral veins, and sympathetic plexuses toward the foramen magnum. The transverse process of C7 transmits only accessory vertebral veins, as the vertebral artery enters at C6.
steps.say: Every cervical vertebra is identified by a foramen transversarium in each transverse process. In C1 through C6, this aperture transmits the ascending vertebral artery and sympathetic plexuses. The C7 foramen carries only accessory veins, since the artery enters at C6.

rows: Costal facets on body and transverse process
Massive kidney body, no costal facets

steps.tx: Thoracic vertebrae articulate with ribs via costal facets on their bodies and transverse processes, displaying heart-shaped bodies. In contrast, a typical **lumbar vertebra** possesses a massive kidney-shaped body without costal facets or foramina transversaria. Its thick quadrilateral spinous process projects horizontally backward, creating wide interlaminar windows suitable for spinal needle entry.
steps.say: Thoracic vertebrae bear costal facets for rib articulations. In contrast, a typical lumbar vertebra possesses a massive kidney-shaped body devoid of costal facets. Its broad quadrilateral spinous process projects horizontally, creating wide interspinous gaps for needle access.

steps.tx: A congenital anomaly occurring in roughly one percent of individuals is the presence of an anomalous **cervical rib**, arising from the anterior tubercle of the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra. It can compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) and the subclavian artery, causing thoracic outlet syndrome with wasting of intrinsic hand muscles.
steps.say: A cervical rib arises from the costal element of the seventh cervical vertebra in about one percent of individuals. This supernumerary rib can compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and subclavian artery, triggering thoracic outlet syndrome with intrinsic hand wasting.

steps.tx: Regional facet orientation governs kinematics: cervical facets lie at forty-five degrees permitting universal motion, thoracic facets lie in the coronal plane permitting rotation, and lumbar facets lie in the sagittal plane permitting flexion and extension. The **fifth lumbar vertebra** features the largest body and massive transverse processes that anchor the robust iliolumbar ligaments.
steps.say: Facet alignment determines mobility: cervical facets slope at forty-five degrees, thoracic facets lie in the coronal plane for rotation, and lumbar facets face sagittally for flexion and extension. The fifth lumbar vertebra bears the largest body and anchors iliolumbar ligaments.
